summary: For ages 10–11: read, write, order and compare whole numbers up to 10,000,000 and state the value of each digit. The core difficulty is the three-digit PERIOD structure (ones, thousands, millions) and holding placeholder zeros (e.g. 7,045,200). Learners should build numbers, translate fluently between numeral, words and expanded form, state digit values as place value (the 7 in 7,045,200 is 'seven million'), and order by a most-significant-digit-first scan with periods aligned, resolving ties one place at a time.
misconceptions: Misreading placeholder zeros — reading 7,045,200 as 'seven hundred forty-five thousand two hundred' by dropping empty places
Losing period boundaries and reading digit-by-digit for very large numbers
Confusing face value with place value (the 7 as 'seven' not 'seven million')
Assuming more digits always means larger without aligning periods when digit counts match
Inserting or omitting 'and' / mis-segmenting when writing in words

activities.title: Period builder with live three-way echo
steps: Set each digit onto a place-value chart labelled Millions | Thousands | Ones, grouped into three-digit periods.

As each digit is placed, watch the number appear three ways at once: the comma-grouped numeral (e.g. 7,045,200), the words read period by period ('seven million, forty-five thousand, two hundred'), and the expanded form.

Deliberately build numbers with internal and cross-period placeholder zeros (e.g. set the hundred-thousands place — the leading digit of the thousands period — to 0, as in 7,045,200) and observe how the words panel skips the empty place without dropping the period boundary.
State aloud, for a chosen digit, its full place value (e.g. 'the 7 is worth seven million').
activities.insight: The comma/period grouping — not the raw digit count — is what lets you read a large number aloud; each nonzero three-digit period is read as a number then given its period name (the ones period has no spoken name, and a period that is all zeros, as in 7,000,200, is skipped entirely), and an internal zero silently holds a column without being spoken.

activities.title: Write, value and order on paper (consolidation)
steps: Write 4,302,561 in words (answer: four million, three hundred two thousand, five hundred sixty-one).
State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200 (answer: seven million).
For the ordering, align the numbers by place and compare left-to-right, moving right only when digits tie; say which digit finally decided between 3,204,000 and 3,240,000.
activities.insight: Reading, writing, valuing and ordering seven-digit numbers all rely on the same period structure and on place-by-place comparison, including when leading digits agree.

activities.title: Labelled reference number with tap-to-reveal periods
steps: Study a labelled seven-digit number (e.g. 4,302,561) and tap each three-digit period to reveal its name and read-out.
Tap an individual digit to reveal its place value.
Use this as a reference anchor while writing or ordering other numbers.
activities.insight: A clearly period-labelled example makes the millions/thousands/ones structure and per-digit place values visible as a stable reference.

activities.title: Dictation and 'why isn't the zero spoken?' discussion
steps: Listen to a mentor dictate a large number in words and write it as a comma-grouped numeral.
Explain why a placeholder zero (e.g. in 7,045,200) is not spoken yet must still be written.
Discuss how the comma/period breaks map to the spoken words.
activities.insight: Articulating why an internal zero holds a place without being spoken is intended to support and strengthen the learner's grasp of the period structure.

checkQuestion: Three tasks on paper. (1) Write 4,302,561 in words. (2) State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200. (3) Order these smallest to largest: 3,240,000; 3,204,000; 3,024,000; 3,420,000.
checkAnswer: (1) four million, three hundred two thousand, five hundred sixty-one. (2) seven million. (3) 3,024,000; 3,204,000; 3,240,000; 3,420,000.
